Eschers Theorem

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: move one corner and watch a special hexagon and three lines keep their surprising properties.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, 120° angles, the meeting point, hexagon copies and the Napoleon triangles.
Look for the math

M. C. Escher used a six-sided tile that fits with copies of itself. J. F. Rigby turned the observation into a theorem: once two corners of a triangle are built from an equilateral triangle by 120° turns, the third 120° turn happens by itself, and three long lines meet at one point.

Build the moving triangle

The yellow points A′, B′, C′ are the corners of a fixed equilateral triangle. Put B anywhere. Turn B around A′ by 120° to get C, and turn C around B′ by 120° to get A. Then A′B = A′C and B′A = B′C, and the turn at C′ comes out as 120° too. Drag a handle and the other two corners are rebuilt the same way the applet rebuilt them. Rigby noted that all three turns must go the same way round the triangle; the logic test flips one turn and the three lines no longer meet.

Six corners that tile the plane

The hexagon A C′ B A′ C B′ is the tile. Turning a whole hexagon by 120° about any of its corners gives another copy, so copies fit edge to edge without gaps: this is the tessellation in the page's second claim. The port creates exactly the 138 copies the applet's three rotation patterns create, and the logic test checks that every one has the same six side lengths. Tick tessellation and hint to see how this grows out of the Napoleon picture.

Why the three lines meet

Build Napoleon triangles on the sides of ABC: their outer tips are A″, B″, C″ (tick hint). The centres of those three triangles are A′, B′, C′, which is why A′B′C′ is equilateral. That ABC and A′B′C′ are in perspective — AA′, BB′, CC′ meet in one point — is the content of Kiepert's theorem. The page's claim held at every one of the 1,575 dragged positions the logic test tried; the meeting point can be far outside the picture.

Not the Ceva–Menelaus applet

That sister applet fixes how points divide the sides and asks when three other lines meet, using an equation in barycentric coordinates. Here no ratio is typed in: the whole triangle moves, and the two facts to check are the 120° turns and the common point of AA′, BB′, CC′. Both pages draw Escher-like tilings, but the claims and the controls are different.

Try ticking hint and tessellation together, then drag A slowly: the coloured tiles swing around while the three marked angles stay at 120°.
